What the D7 is
The D7 is the name most people use for Portugal's
residence visa for retirees, religious workers and people living on their own income

(in Portuguese, “visto de residência para a fixação de residência de reformados, religiosos e pessoas que vivam de rendimentos”). It is for non-EU citizens who want to live in Portugal on a pension or on regular passive income: rent, dividends, interest, royalties and similar. It is not a work visa.
EU, EEA and Swiss citizens don't need it: they register their residence locally instead.
You apply at the Portuguese consulate or visa centre that covers where you live legally. The visa itself is valid for
four months and two entries
. Within that time you have to ask AIMA (the Agency for Integration, Migration and Asylum) for a residence permit (“título de residência”) in Portugal (
MNE: visa types
How much income you need in 2026
Portugal doesn't publish a fixed euro amount for the D7. The rule is a percentage of the national minimum wage (RMMG), set by
Portaria n.º 1563/2007
first adult: 100% of the minimum wage;
each additional adult: 50%;
each child under 18, or adult child who depends on you: 30%.
The minimum wage for mainland Portugal in 2026 is
€920 a month
Decreto-Lei n.º 139/2025
). The consular portal applies the same €920 figure (

; also
AIMA

These are our own arithmetic from the official percentages. The minimum wage normally changes every January, so the numbers change with it. Consulates can ask for more, and many look at the whole picture, not just the minimum.
Article 5(6) of the same Portaria says these means must be secured for
at least 12 months

and shown to be available in Portugal. For one adult, 12 × €920 = €11,040. This is why applicants are usually asked to show funds in a Portuguese bank account. Your consulate's checklist says exactly what proof it accepts.
Documents the consulate asks for
The official checklist for this visa (
MNE, English
Portuguese
) asks for:
Retirees:
proof of the pension amount, and proof that you receive it or have other income available in Portugal.
Passive income:
proof of income from movable or immovable property, intellectual property or financial investments, and proof that it is available in Portugal.
A statement of responsibility (“termo de responsabilidade”) where it applies.

The general documents for every national visa are also needed: the application form, two passport photos, and a passport valid for at least three months beyond the planned stay. There are more items on the
general documentation page
. Consulates often add their own requirements, such as accommodation in Portugal, health or travel insurance, or a criminal record certificate.
Check the official page of your own consulate or visa centre
before you book.
Family members can apply at the same time with a “visto de residência para acompanhamento de requerente de visto de residência” (a residence visa to accompany the main applicant).
The steps, in order
Get a Portuguese tax number (NIF). You will need it for a bank account and a lease. See our NIF guide.
Open a Portuguese bank account and move enough funds in. The amounts are above.
Collect the documents on your consulate's checklist. Translations and apostilles are often required, so check which.
Apply at the consulate or visa centre and pay the visa fee.
Check the official page
for the current fee and processing times.
Travel to Portugal while the four-month visa is valid and attend your AIMA appointment for the residence permit.
After that comes the residence permit. Under the Foreigners' Law, a temporary residence permit is generally valid for two years and can then be renewed for three-year periods (
AIMA: residence permits
). Check AIMA for how and where renewals are handled at the moment.
What changed recently

changed the Foreigners' Law in October 2025. One change affects family reunification after you arrive: in general it now needs two years of valid residence, with exceptions such as minor children. If family members aren't applying with you from the start, read the current rules on
aima.gov.pt
or ask a qualified lawyer before you plan around reunification.

Quick answers
How much money do I need for the Portugal D7 visa in 2026?

The rule is 100% of the minimum wage for the main applicant, 50% for each extra adult and 30% for each child. With the 2026 minimum wage of €920, that is €920 a month for one person and €1,380 for a couple. The means must be secured for at least 12 months: for one person, 12 × €920 = €11,040. Always check your consulate's checklist.
Can I work on a D7 visa?
The D7 is meant for people living on pensions or passive income. If your income comes from remote work for clients or an employer outside Portugal, look at the
D8
instead. For anything else, ask the consulate or a qualified professional.
Where do I apply for the D7?
At the Portuguese consulate or visa centre for the country where you live legally. After you arrive in Portugal, AIMA handles the residence permit.

What the D8 is
The D8 is Portugal's visa for
remote work done for employers or clients outside Portugal
, often called the digital nomad visa. It is for non-EU citizens. There are two versions (
Temporary stay visa
(“visto de estada temporária para o exercício de atividade profissional prestada de forma remota”): for stays of up to a year.
Residence visa
(“visto de residência … nómada digital”): for moving to Portugal. It is valid for four months and two entries, and in that time you ask AIMA for a residence permit.
The legal basis is article 61.º-B of the Foreigners' Law (Lei n.º 23/2007). The document list is in

What is the income requirement for the Portugal D8 visa in 2026?
Average monthly income over the last three months of at least four times the minimum wage. With the 2026 minimum wage of €920, that is €3,680 a month. It rises when the minimum wage rises.
Can I work for Portuguese clients on a D8?
The D8 is for work done remotely for employers or clients outside Portugal. If you plan to work for Portuguese companies, ask the consulate or a qualified professional which visa fits.
Is the D8 the same as the D7?
No. The
is for pensions and passive income, at 100% of the minimum wage for one adult. The D8 is for active remote work, at four times the minimum wage.

You can do a D8 application yourself using the official pages linked above. For the day you land, these are useful: mobile data before you get a Portuguese SIM, and a pre-booked transfer from Porto airport if you arrive with luggage.
Portugal D7 visa (passive income)
No. The D7 is for pensions and passive income, at 100% of the minimum wage for one adult. The D8 is for active remote work, at four times the minimum wage.
Évora day trip from Lisbon by train | Day in Portugal
Évora in a day from Lisbon: which Intercidades trains from Oriente, Entrecampos or Sete Rios make a there-and-back, and the Roman temple from the square.
Évora day trip — book the Intercidades seat
Évora day trip
From Lisbon · the Alentejo
Évora in a day: one Intercidades out, one back, and the temple from the square.

Évora is not a metro ride. CP runs a handful of Intercidades trains, the seat is reserved, and the useful ones are in the morning out and the late afternoon back. If your date is not on the sheet, do not invent a midday departure. Go another day, or stay in Lisbon.
The Roman temple in Évora, columns standing in the open square
Photo: Norbert Nagel,
The trains that make a day

The CP sheet “Intercidades / Regional, Linha do Alentejo”, in force since 6 September 2026, lists through trains from Lisboa Oriente to Évora. Two morning examples: 07:02 from Oriente, 08:47 into Évora (1 hour 45); 09:02 from Oriente, 10:45 into Évora (1 hour 43). The same trains call at Entrecampos and Sete Rios a few minutes after Oriente — 07:10 and 07:14 on the 07:02, 09:10 and 09:14 on the 09:02 — so you do not have to start at the airport station.

Coming back, that sheet lists departures from Évora at 07:00, 09:14, 11:30, 16:51 and 19:14. A day in town is a morning train out and the 16:51 or the 19:14 back. The 11:30 is too early if you only arrived at 10:45.
The remarks column matters more than the clock. CP marks some trains Monday–Friday except public holidays, and some Saturday, Sunday and public holidays. The PDF is
comboios Lisboa–Évora–Beja
. Buy the seat on
. There is no walk-up urban train every 20 minutes on this line. Check before you go, including the fare, which is on the booking page and not repeated here.
What the day is for

The walled centre is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and it is walkable from the station without a taxi for the temple and the squares. The Roman temple — often called the Temple of Diana — stands in the open. You see it from the square. You do not need a ticket to stand there.

The cathedral is the paid interior, up the hill from the temple. The church of São Francisco keeps the Capela dos Ossos, the chapel lined with bones. Both charge at the door; the price is on the desk that day, so check it there rather than from a blog. If you only have the hours between 10:45 and 16:51, do the square, the temple, one church, lunch, and the walk back to the station. A second village is how you miss the train.
Train, unless the day is bigger than Évora

For the walled centre the Intercidades is the whole transport plan. A hire car is for adding a village or a wine estate the train does not stop at, and then someone is driving back to Lisbon in the dark. If that is the trip:
compare cars from local Lisbon rental firms
Bags if you are on the 19:14 and the hotel will not hold them:
luggage storage in Lisbon
How long is the train from Lisbon to Évora?
About 1 hour 40 to 1 hour 45 on the Intercidades. The CP timetable since 6 September 2026 times 07:02 from Lisboa Oriente to 08:47 in Évora, and 09:02 to 10:45. Not every train runs every day.
Do you need a car?
Not for the centre. You need a reserved seat on the right train, and a return that still exists on your date.
Is the Roman temple free?
It stands in a public square. You look at it without a ticket. The cathedral and the Capela dos Ossos are indoors and charged.

Lisbon airport to the city: metro, taxi or transfer | Day in Portugal
How to get from Lisbon airport (LIS) to the centre: red-line metro to Saldanha, taxi, or a pre-booked transfer, and when each makes sense.
Lisbon airport to the centre — metro, taxi or transfer
Humberto Delgado Airport (LIS)
From Lisbon airport to your bed, without a taxi you do not need.

The airport station is on the red line, inside the walk from Terminal 1 arrivals. For most people that is the whole transfer. A pre-booked car earns its price late at night, with children, or with more bags than hands.
Three ways in
Metro, taxi, pre-booked car
1. Metro, red line.

Metropolitano de Lisboa’s airport page times Aeroporto to Saldanha (it calls Saldanha the centre) at 18 minutes and €1.92. A taxi, without traffic, is 20–30 minutes and €16–19. The page says every journey time is approximate. Checked 6 November 2026 on
metrolisboa.pt
. Check before you go.

From arrivals at Terminal 1, follow the metro signs. The same page says a contactless bank card, phone or watch works on the validator, so you do not have to buy a paper ticket first. Saldanha is the stop if you are sleeping on Avenida. For Baixa-Chiado, change to the green line. Oriente, for the Évora train, is also on the red line, before Saldanha.
2. Taxi from the rank.
The €16–19 figure above is the metro company’s comparison for a ride without traffic, not a quote from a driver. Ask before the bags go in the boot.
3. Pre-booked transfer.
A fixed price and a name at arrivals. The calm choice when the metro is a bad idea.

How do I get from Lisbon airport to the centre?

Red-line metro from the Aeroporto station to Saldanha, about 18 minutes and €1.92 on Metropolitano de Lisboa’s airport page, checked 6 November 2026. Change lines for Baixa-Chiado. Times on that page are approximate.
When is a pre-booked car worth it?
A late landing, children, or more bags than you can carry onto a metro. Otherwise the red line is the transfer.
Should I rent a car at the airport?
If you are leaving Lisbon, not if you are staying in it. Pena and the Moorish Castle do not allow private cars on the access roads.

Where to stay in Lisbon: Baixa, Alfama, Belém | Day in Portugal
Where to stay in Lisbon: Baixa, Chiado, Alfama, Príncipe Real, Avenida and Saldanha, or Belém — and which one to sleep in.
Lisbon · a bed
Sleep where the hill is a choice, not a surprise.
Six neighbourhoods, six different ways to end the evening. Pick the one that matches the station you will actually use.
Arcades along Praça do Comércio in the Baixa, Lisbon
Baixa

The flat grid between Rossio and the river, rebuilt after 1755. Right if you want Rua Augusta under the window and the Rossio trains to Sintra a short walk away. Rua Augusta itself is a parade at night. Sleep a street back.
Largo do Chiado in Lisbon, the square above the Baixa
Photo: Ardfern,
Chiado
Up the hill from Baixa, still central, with the bookshops and the evening streets. Steeper than the grid, quieter than Alfama’s tram lane. A fair base for three walking days.
A sloping street of tiled houses in Alfama, Lisbon
Photo: Matti Blume,
Alfama
The postcard and the hills. Fine for one night if the room is off the 28E route and off the miradouro bars. A bad week if every return is a staircase with a suitcase.
The garden at Príncipe Real in Lisbon
Photo: CorreiaPM, public domain, via
Our pick
Príncipe Real
The garden, a walk down to Chiado, and evenings that are still a neighbourhood. This is where we would sleep for three nights of walking, if the rate is honest.
A Lisbon metro train at Aeroporto station, on the red line toward São Sebastião
Avenida and Saldanha

The red line from the airport reaches Saldanha with no change. Metropolitano de Lisboa times that ride at about 18 minutes. Flatter, more of a city than a lane in Alfama. Right if you land late or you are done with cobbles. The photo is the airport station, which is the reason to stay up here.
Belém Tower beside the Tagus
Belém

The monastery and the tower on day 2 without a commute, and a Cascais-line train back to Cais do Sodré when you want the centre. Quiet at night. Far from Alfama on foot, which is either the appeal or the mistake.
Search those neighbourhoods, not “best hotel Lisbon”. Filter by cancellation, and by the walk to Rossio, Cais do Sodré, or a metro stop you will use twice a day.
